subject: Banking
title: Small Business Lending Fees
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Small Business Lending Fees.

hook.text: Small business loans charge 6-13% interest plus origination fees of 1-5%. A $100,000 loan costs $5,000 just to open.

buildup.text: Banks consider small businesses risky. Higher rates and fees compensate for the chance the business fails.

discovery.text: SBA-guaranteed loans reduce bank risk. The government covers 75-85% of losses, yet banks still charge full rates.

twist.text: Big banks approve only 13% of small business loan requests. Community banks approve 49%.

climax.text: Small business lending is high-margin, high-risk. Banks profit from fees and rates that reflect risk they've often.

punchline.text: High rates plus fees plus government guarantees. Banks profit while risk shifts.

quiz.question: What approval rate do big banks have for small business loans?

details.summary: Small business loans generate substantial fee income for banks through origination charges, SBA loan guaranty fees, annual renewal fees, and prepayment penalties that can add 2 to 5 percent to the total cost of borrowing.
details.whyItMatters: Small businesses are critical to the economy, and the cost of their financing directly affects job creation and growth. High loan fees can make the difference between a small business surviving or failing.
takeaways: Origination fees on small business loans range from 1 to 5 percent
SBA loan fees include guaranty fees of 2-3.5 percent of the guaranteed portion
Annual review and maintenance fees add recurring costs beyond interest

faq.question: What fees do small businesses pay beyond interest?
faq.answer: Beyond interest, businesses face origination fees of 1-5%, annual maintenance fees, packaging fees for SBA loans, appraisal costs, legal fees, and sometimes prepayment penalties. These can add 2-5 percentage points to the effective cost of the loan.

faq.question: Why are small business loan fees higher than consumer loan fees?
faq.answer: Small business loans require more underwriting work, financial analysis, and ongoing monitoring. Default rates are also higher than consumer mortgages. Banks price fees to cover these costs, though the fees also serve as a significant profit center.
